summary:
CALL OF SPACE is an game interactive educational space exploration simulator designed to make space science and technology more accessible through an immersive, hands-on experience.

The project allows users to experience the different stages of a space mission : selecting a destination, defining objectives, designing and equipping a spacecraft, inspecting its systems, managing resources, launching a rocket, navigating through space and exploring destinations such as the Moon, Mars and asteroids. It features customizable manual flight controls and an automatic piloting system.

Our vision is to make this experience accessible across multiple platforms, including PC, mobile devices and Virtual Reality (VR), offering different levels of interaction and immersion.

CALL OF SPACE introduces essential concepts such as propulsion, orbital mechanics, spacecraft engineering and mission management.

By transforming complex scientific concepts into interactive experiences, the project addresses the challenge through hands-on learning, experimentation, decision-making and problem-solving. Its ultimate goal is to inspire younger generations to explore science, technology and space exploration.
details:
CALL OF SPACE is an educational space mission design game. Players choose one of five missions (lunar exploration, Mars, station maintenance, asteroid exploration, and space rescue), then assemble their spacecraft from eleven subsystems: engine, booster, fuel tank, structure, command, power, communications, navigation, science, crew, and life support. Every choice has a cost in mass, propellant, and energy, and must stay within the mission budget. Players then complete a pre-flight checklist, ignite the engines, and fly the ascent using thrust and pitch controls. A final mission report shows whether the mission was a complete success, a partial success, or a failure, and recommends what to change next time.

The goal is to teach space engineering through practice, without prior training. The game is aimed at students and the general public. The data is real: Earth–Moon and Earth–Mars distances come from JPL Horizons, and the data for asteroid 2012 TC4 comes from JPL’s Small-Body Database. The NASA photographs used in the application are credited within it.

The project is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite, and styled with Tailwind CSS. The interface is available in English, French, and German. In the current version, multiplayer is simulated; online multiplayer, a mobile version, and a VR version are planned.

The expected impact is a better understanding of engineering trade-offs (mass, fuel, energy, budget) among young people and students, and a reusable learning tool for teachers. The game is intentionally presented as an educational demonstration, not as technical advice or real mission planning.
